I was just finishing up an early morning eye appointment at a nice strip mall in my area, an affluent white-majority place. Beautiful keystone arches, clean establishments with high-end modern interior design, and cool autumn colors. Realizing I didn't eat and knowing one of my favorite fast food places was next door, JJ's sandwiches, I decided to check if it was open. It was 9:30 am on a weekend, but I figured any food service industry would be serving at this hour.

I leave my appointment and I see a black employee inside, stuffed into a tight apron. He had a neat beard and clear eyes, additionally was well-fed and in decent shape. He was standing behind the counter looking at his phone in disposable gloves (unsanitary, by the way) probably taking a moment to himself during the process of preparing ingredients for the day. Store hours were listed to be half an hour from that point, but I knock on the glass politely to see if he'd be willing to do a favor by serving me early. He unlocks the door and peers halfway out with a blank expression. "Yeah?"

"Hey, I know you guys aren't open, but was wondering if I could buy a sandwich really quickly," I say.

"Nah, man. I can't. Sorry," which felt genuine enough. Corporate rules come first, why risk it? I thank him anyway and go on my way, deciding to stop off at the first place open: McDonald's. It's a typical box establishment with a terrible parking lot that looks like it's shoved into the most inconvenient but busy zoned area as possible. There are random rails outside the landing outside the restaurant, being just inconvenient enough to annoy. I go in and a surly black lady with her greasy stringy hair shoved into her hat is taking orders. She moves through the customers quickly, and luckily I know my order when I go to these ticky tacky burger factories. As disgusting as the grease and sanitation are, the food tastes really great. I order, but it's the morning menu, so no luck. (I loathe people who designate specific types of foods for certain meals, but I know it's the social norm.)

I step back and let the line of two or so orders go ahead of me and look at the menu for a while. The girl behind the counter looks annoyed like it's typical of a white person to not know about ordering fast food at different times of the day. A few minutes of debating to myself go by, but I land on an egg McMuffin because I've only heard good things about it from various socioeconomic classes. When I finally get my food a few moments later, I go out to my car to eat, wanting to avoid any "encounters."

I dig into the bag and bite into it. Instant disgust, it's dry and spongey; nothing at all like French Toast, with no flavor or sugar powdered on. (Syrup is for Canadians and Aunt Jemimahs.) No wonder black people are bitter if this is a fine culinary experience in their area; fast food is peddled to them like crack. Luckily I was smart enough to get a hashbrown patty as well, a food you can't really fuck up as long as it's hot. Even though it was as good as expected, I could buy a huge frozen pack and microwave the same thing at home in a minute for a quarter of the cost.

What's the point of this story? Manners and understanding are important when not getting your way! Would a sheboon ghetto queen have accepted a morning menu order without complaint if she wanted a burger? How long would a held-back teen athlete have spent staring at the menu deadpan without thinking of the people behind him? Would the employees have tried to make an exception for a black person? How long would they argue back and forth? Would it end in a fight and cuffs? The answer is probably no, but I've worked as a pawnbroker before. I can tell you the answer is "yes" often enough that race prejudice is still alive and well for a reason.

By analogy, let’s imagine that a retailer furniture company were in a position to offload all their shipping costs to the trucking industry. By government decree, the truckers were not permitted to charge any more or less whether they were shipping one chair or a whole houseful of furniture.

This is where I get lost on the issue because I've already paid the mover for moving costs. My moving contract says unlimited and that's what I expect, not Netflix at 780p because Netflix won't pay additional moving costs. How can the mover turn around and ask for more money from the seller to move product and shipping costs I've already paid for?

I should get to choose how to use those prepaid moving costs and what gets moved. If, in my astronomical monthly cable bill, I pay for unlimited bandwidth, that's what I expect to receive. They can't offer to move unlimited content then burn the loading dock on the other side.

You haven't already paid for the moving costs, though. Not really. Furntiure buyers don't pay a monthly fee to recieve as much furniture as they want. But most internet customers do pay their ISP a set amount for the internet even if the amount of data being moved through the system increases.

Back to shipping for a second. As the amount of things being shipped increases, the costs of moving everything goes up. The shipper needs more trucks, more drivers, larger facilities, more fuel, et cetera. The shipper can either charge more to the end customer to receive shipments or more to the shipper to pay for the increased costs of shipping. You don't pay the shipper a one time fee to receive as much from a shipper as you want. You pay for what you receive. So, with shipping, the additional costs are borne buy the receivers allowing those receiving more to pay more.

With the internet, this means Comcast would charge Netflix customers more than non-Netflix customers. Instead, Comcast suggests charging Netflix more. For some reason many customers have been convinced Comcast should be the one to pay without charging more to either their customers or Netflix. Comcast thinks rather than charge all of its customers more, Netflix should subsidize Netflix's customers by paying for a fast lane. Frankly, I don't particularly care about either Comcast or Netflix and don't see why I shouldn't let them sort it out. At the end of the day I am an intended beneficiary of both of them, not just one or the other.

I think my primary concern is having my streaming video throttled while two multi-billion dollar companies have a pissing contest over fees (e.g. Dish and CBS recently), all while I'm paying full price for a service I'm not getting. Net neutrality prevented this scenario. Now, nothing does?
